b: The Department of Philosophy at Trinity College in Hartford, Connecticut has adopted a new policy banning students from using AI in classrooms or for coursework.

Deliberate use of AI in philosophy courses, in any capacity and for any purpose, is forbidden. This includes, but is not limited to: using AI to summarize reading assignments; using it to “brainstorm” and come up with ideas; as a research tool for presentations or oral examinations, or as a tool to aid in the writing or editing process (e.g., research, drafting, editing, compiling a bibliography, etc.). Philosophy is focused on cultivating our abilities to think, to read, to write, to speak, to reason, and to live ethically. AI undermines all of these goals.
According to the Trinity Tripod, the faculty vote in favor of the policy was unanimous.
Shane Ewegen, a professor in the Philosophy Department, told the student newspaper:

Ultimately, we wanted to avoid having six different AI policies that contradict each other. So after having some discussion about our attitudes and understandings of AI—and the dangers that it’s posing to thinking and the ability of students to think—we were able, after some back and forth, to agree upon a single blanket policy, which simply forbids the use of AI in any capacity in any philosophy course.

Professor Ewegen has also led a faculty movement to encourage Trinity College to divest from AI software companies, which resulted in a letter from faculty to the college administration about AI policy, the Tripod reports:

“We, the below signatories, request that Trinity College immediately and thoroughly divest from AI companies and the software companies that support them. The technology is too fresh, too unregulated, too dangerous and too unpredictable to safely integrate into the college’s operations. Currently, the support of such technology is incommensurate with Trinity’s stated commitments to fostering intellectual and ethical growth, to protecting the environment, and to building and protecting a safe future for the next generation,” the letter reads. It also requests that the administration take “a firm, immediate, and public stance against such technologies” until they have been deemed safe for academic use, “if [such a] time ever comes,” and that future AI policy be subject to faculty vote.

Regarding the Philosophy Department ban on AI use, Ewegen says, “So part of what our hope was, at least my hope, in adopting a policy like this, is to get more faculty and more students, and hopefully more administrators, to think a bit more critically about the role that this technology is playing in academia right now and the distinct threats that it poses.”
Have other philosophy departments enacted similar policies?

UPDATE: I asked if the policy also applied to faculty. Professor Ewegen wrote, “Currently, at least, it applies to all of the philosophy faculty. (None of us use AI or want to.) Were we to hire new faculty members, we would not impose it upon them; instead, we would talk with them about their position vis a vis AI and invite them to revise the policy with us.”
